name: Vijayanathar Temple, Tiruvijayamangai
deity: Shiva as Vijayanathar (Vijayanatheswarar), with the goddess Mangalanayaki (Mangalambikai)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of Chola Nadu on the northern bank of the Kaveri, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); a temple in the medieval Chola manner
summary: Vijayanathar Temple at Tiruvijayamangai is a Tevaram shrine of the Kaveri's northern bank, remembered as the place where Arjuna, also called Vijaya, won the Pashupata weapon from Shiva.

sections.history: Tiruvijayamangai lies in the Thanjavur district, in the old Chola heartland north of the Kaveri, where a long chain of Shiva shrines was sung by the Tevaram saints. This temple is one of them, praised in the hymns of Sambandar and Appar, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The name carries the story: Vijaya is another name of Arjuna, the Pandava archer, and the Lord here is Vijayanathar, the master of his victory. The shrine is built in the manner of the medieval Chola temples and has been kept in worship by the village around it for many centuries, though no firm record of its founder or founding date has come down to us.
sections.architecture: This is a compact temple in the Chola manner, whose charm lies in its quiet scale rather than in monumental towers. The sanctum houses the Shiva linga, worshipped as self-manifested, and tradition points to a scar on its surface, the mark of Arjuna's blow in the encounter that gave the temple its name. The goddess Mangalanayaki is worshipped here as the Lord's consort. Close by lies the Arjuna Teertham, the sacred tank named for the hero whose penance is remembered here, where devotees bathe and sit in quiet before entering the shrine.
sections.legends: The legend of Tiruvijayamangai belongs to the Mahabharata. On Krishna's counsel, Arjuna came to this place to perform severe penance, seeking Shiva's grace and the divine weapon known as the Pashupatastra. While he sat in meditation, a demon named Mukasura came to disturb him, and Shiva appeared before the warrior in the guise of a hunter. A contest followed between the archer and the hunter. Pleased by Arjuna's courage, devotion and steadiness, the Lord revealed himself with the goddess and placed the Pashupatastra in his hands. Local belief holds that the scar of that encounter can still be seen on the linga, and from it the Lord takes the name Vijayanathar.
sections.festivals: The great festival of the temple is Maha Shivaratri, kept in the Tamil month of Masi (February to March), when the village gathers through the night for worship of Vijayanathar. The monthly Pradosham is observed here as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar and smaller village temples may keep a modest festival calendar.
sections.experience: Tiruvijayamangai rewards a quiet, unhurried visit. It is a village temple, far from the crowds of the larger Kaveri shrines, and the stillness of the surrounding fields is part of its charm. Begin at the Arjuna Teertham, then come to the sanctum of Vijayanathar and look for the mark on the linga that tradition ties to Arjuna's encounter, before turning to the goddess Mangalanayaki. Many devotees come to pray for success in their undertakings, as the Lord's name suggests, and the story of the archer who won grace through penance gives the visit a quiet encouragement of its own.

visit.timings: Typically open from about 8:00 a.m. to noon and again from about 5:00 p.m. to 7:00 p.m.; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple stands in the village of Tiruvijayamangai, now known as Govindaputhur, in the Kumbakonam area of Thanjavur district, roughly 11 to 13 km from Kumbakonam, which is the nearest railway station. Buses run toward the village, and visitors can alight at Govindaputhur, from where the temple is a short walk. Tiruchirappalli is the nearest major airport. Local auto-rickshaws or a hired car from Kumbakonam make the visit easiest, and the nearby Thiruvaikavur temple can be combined in the same day.
